title: A ? of When with Panda Bear
summary: Pete Kember discusses A ? of When, his collaboration with Panda Bear, Jamaican musical influences and making music with hope for the future. He also reflects on radio and record stores as places to discover music.
transcript:
Pete Kember was one of the original co-founders of that highly influential UK band alongside Jason Pierce who had a quite sort of famous falling out, the two of them with the band dissolving in 1991.

Famously, Pete Kember and Jason Pierce recorded the tracks from their final record together as Spacemen 3 recurring in separate studios, splitting the vinyl down the middle with one side dedicated to each artist.

And, yeah, Jason Pierce going on, of course, to form Spiritualized.

And since Spacemen 3, Pete Kember has really continuously pushed the boundaries of different monikers like Spectrum and E.A.R.

and, of course, as Sonic Boom.

He's also been the secret weapon in the producer's chair for massive records by MGMT and Beach House.

And, of course, Panda Bear, Noah Lennox from the groundbreaking Animal Collective, who we just heard from earlier.

Pete's collaborative partnership with Noah Lennox goes back to 2011 with Pete co-producing Panda Bear's Tomboy Record and also his 2015 release, Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper.

The two icons of psychedelic pop are both based in Portugal, Noah for the last two decades, and Pete Kember for over a decade now.

And they've combined their brilliant musical minds on two collaborative albums together now, 2022's Reset, and now with their most recent offering called A Question of When, which is an album that famously the band have not made available via streaming services.

There's no music videos.

It is a very intentional decision by the band to keep things in their words IRL rather than URL, with the goal for the music to create physical connections between people and to encourage them to enjoy a real experience in the world and with each other.

The new record, A Question of When, they've said is a deliberate choice to use sounds and textures that they haven't used before, almost as a sonic reset after their reset record in a way.

It's still another total sonic playground, though.

They've packed in everything from Mary Lattimore's harp loops to steel drums to yodelling and even bits of a mariachi band as well.

And yeah, while it sounds incredibly dreamy, the tracks are actually sort of diving into some heavy themes like online exhaustion and climate anxiety as well.

So I began the interview by asking Pete Kember if they sort of intentionally leaned on these more uplifting sonic textures to act as more of an optimistic counterweight to the darker subject matter that they're writing about.

Yeah, absolutely.

And it was the same with reset.

We're dealing with some tricky issues in reset, but it was something that we talked about before starting working together as Panda Bear and Sonic Boom.

I was talking with Noah about how I always was really impressed by Jamaican music from the mid and late 60s, that they were dealing with some super tough issues in Jamaica.

Everything was collapsing and crashing.

There's just some amazing music that came out of that era and presented in a very positive way, even though they're talking about not being able to get food and not being able to, you know, having massive inflation and where their money's not worth anything.

And they're singing songs about these police and thieves.

The Junior Murvin track would be a good example.

They're talking about tough issues, but in a really beautiful, positive way.

So we went into the whole thing of working together with that as one of our touchstones.

Would you say, like, the record overall is a hopeful record?

Yeah, I think you have to be a little realistic when you can look out into the world around you and see what's going on.

It's very hard not to let that enter your consciousness, but I think you have to be positive and be looking for ways that things can be different.

Most of the problems on this planet are caused by all of us.

And so it's really all of us who have to act if we want to change that and see things different.

We think someone's going to come along and wave a magic wand.

God forbid a politician.

Then, yeah, there is no positivity if you believe that.

But if you believe that humans can make good, I think you have to have some positivity.
